rationale: This qualitative empirical study (interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists in Khayelitsha, Cape Town) directly examines household/community sanitation access outcomes (open toilets, bucket disposal, inadequate service provision) and explicitly links inadequate provision to an administrative/tenure classification mechanism (authorities' continued classification of the settlement as 'temporary' and conditional treatment of urban infrastructure entitlements). All eligibility criteria (C1-C4) are clearly satisfied at the Title/Abstract stage.
plain_vs_narrow_note: Both the narrow rule-type and plain/literal readings of Criterion 2 yield an 'include' decision because the abstract explicitly identifies an administrative/tenure classification rule—authorities' continued classification of the informal settlement as 'temporary'—as a mechanism perpetuating inadequate sanitation service provision and conditional access.

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists, supported by computer-assisted coding in ATLAS. ti 22
Testimonies reveal how inadequate sanitation systems, including open toilets, bucket disposal, and stagnant wastewater, exacerbate illness and psychosocial stress in densely packed dwellings.
Although authorities acknowledge the crisis, the continued classification of the settlement as “temporary” perpetuates inadequate service provision and entrenches vulnerability.
